series: The World in / The World Ahead
note: The Economist's own reviews of its previous edition's predictions. economist_says records the publisher's claim (right / wrong / partly), not a Hindsight grade. Quotes are from the review articles.

reviews.reviewer: Niall Ferguson (historian commissioned by the editor; named as author in the World in 2016 index page)
reviews.note: A review of the first 20 editions, commissioned by the editor from an outside historian and published in the issue. It also says The World in 2005 "broke with tradition by admitting that a few of its predictions for 2004 had not come true"; that 2005 review was not found in public form.

claims.quote: Only one contributor was badly wide of the mark: he predicted that Nomura Securities would take over Merrill Lynch.
claims.subject: Japanese takeover of a Wall Street firm (1987)

claims.quote: The obvious political omission was the dramatic collapse of Communist rule in eastern Europe in 1989, which (like so many analysts) TWI did not manage to predict.
claims.subject: Collapse of communism 1989

claims.quote: The Japanese stockmarket crash of 1990 was a bolt from the blue; also unheralded was the 1994-95 Mexican crisis. No one foresaw the Asian crisis of 1997
claims.subject: Financial crises 1990-1998

claims.quote: There was supposed to be a Bush senior election victory in 1992 (Bill Clinton was not even mentioned before becoming president).
claims.subject: US presidential election 1992

claims.quote: And a Middle East peace settlement was foreseen in 1996, as was the failure of the planned European Monetary Union
claims.subject: Middle East peace 1996; European Monetary Union

claims.quote: Other notably bad calls include a Red Sox victory in the World Series (in 1996), a “bloody mess” when Hong Kong was returned to China (in 1997), an “Islamic Reformation” in the Middle East (in 2000), a property-market crash (in 2003) and a sustained Japanese economic recovery (in almost every year since 1990).
claims.subject: Assorted misses 1996-2003

claims.quote: Here the laurels unquestionably belong to Fidel Castro, whose fall from power TWI consistently and vainly predicted in the aftermath of the 1989 revolutions
claims.subject: Fall of Fidel Castro

claims.quote: The World in 1988 foresaw major changes in central Europe, especially in East Germany—a year out, but pretty close.
claims.subject: Change in central Europe (1988)

claims.quote: Anthony King called the 1992 British election correctly as a Tory victory—when most media folk favoured Labour.
claims.subject: UK general election 1992

claims.quote: George Bush junior was identified early (1998) as the next president
claims.subject: US presidential election 2000

claims.quote: TWI confidently predicted Saddam Hussein's fall in 2003 (though it had done the same ten years before). And The World in 2004 got Mr Bush's re-election dead right too.
claims.subject: Fall of Saddam Hussein 2003; US election 2004

claims.quote: The World in 2008 failed to predict any of this.
claims.subject: Global financial crisis 2008

claims.quote: We also failed to foresee Russia's invasion of Georgia
claims.subject: Russian invasion of Georgia

claims.quote: We said the OPEC cartel would aim to keep oil prices in the lofty range of $60-80 a barrel (the price peaked at $147 in July).
claims.subject: Oil price 2008

claims.quote: We thought that Romano Prodi would probably see out the year as prime minister of Italy
claims.subject: Italian prime minister

claims.quote: that Canada would pull its troops out of Afghanistan's Kandahar province (it didn't)
claims.subject: Canadian troops in Kandahar

claims.quote: that Ken Livingstone would be re-elected as mayor of London (he was defeated by his Conservative rival, Boris Johnson)
claims.subject: London mayoral election 2008

claims.quote: Oh, and we expected that by now Hillary Clinton would be heading for the White House.
claims.subject: US presidential election 2008

claims.quote: In America, we expected slumping house prices and a battle to resist recession through government spending, interest-rate cuts and surging exports
claims.subject: US economy 2008

claims.quote: In Asia, we highlighted the froth of the Shanghai Stock Exchange—which fell by two-thirds over the next 12 months.
claims.subject: Shanghai stockmarket

claims.quote: In politics, as expected, José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero won a second term in Spain.
claims.subject: Spanish general election 2008

claims.quote: Vladimir Putin duly retained real power in Russia despite stepping down from the presidency.
claims.subject: Putin retains power

claims.quote: And, as we suggested might happen, the Kuomintang's victory in Taiwan's presidential election opened the way for a resumption of direct flights to and from mainland China.
claims.subject: Taiwan election and cross-strait flights

claims.quote: And we forecast that China would for the first time overtake the United States in the gold-medal table, with Russia in third place.
claims.subject: Beijing Olympics gold-medal table

claims.quote: We missed 2008's extreme financial panic, but expected banks like JPMorgan Chase to expand by acquiring stricken competitors
claims.subject: Bank acquisitions

claims.quote: he offered three catastrophe scenarios which could flow from the country’s chaos and paralysis: a no-deal Brexit, a divisive second referendum, or a lurch to a far-left government.
claims.subject: Brexit scenarios
claims.note: The review calls these "so far, so prescient".

claims.quote: Yet our central scenario—that Britain would leave the European Union as planned on March 31st—proved to be wrong.
claims.subject: Brexit date

claims.quote: we rightly expected America to break its record for uninterrupted growth but amid gathering nervousness about the next recession.
claims.subject: US economic expansion record

claims.quote: We thought India’s growth would accelerate; it did the opposite.
claims.subject: India GDP growth

claims.quote: An early contender for gold was the prediction that a couple of big European banks would merge.
claims.subject: European bank merger
claims.note: The review says the banks announced talks but no merger happened, and awards it "bronze".

claims.quote: the foretelling of the ­developing rivalry between China and America, with its “great wall of distrust” spreading well beyond trade, proved uncannily accurate.
claims.subject: US-China rivalry

claims.quote: And gold? This judge awards it to the prediction that 2019 would be the “year of the vegan”.
claims.subject: Veganism

claims.quote: Missing from the list were important shocks such as mass protests in Hong Kong or a major attack on Saudi Arabia’s oil facilities.
claims.subject: Unforeseen events 2019

claims.quote: Like almost everyone else, we were blindsided by the outbreak of covid-19
claims.subject: Covid-19 pandemic

claims.quote: We expected a global slowdown, but not the biggest economic contraction since the Depression.
claims.subject: Global economy 2020

claims.quote: Donald Trump was, as expected, impeached but not convicted by the Senate.
claims.subject: Trump impeachment

claims.quote: Tsai Ing-wen won re-election as president of Taiwan.
claims.subject: Taiwan presidential election 2020

claims.quote: Sir Keir Starmer, whom we tipped as “a dark horse to watch” in the aftermath of Britain’s general election, became leader of the country's opposition Labour Party after its defeat.
claims.subject: UK Labour leadership

claims.quote: TikTok ended up embroiled in a row between the superpowers, in line with our prediction that more Chinese tech firms, beyond Huawei, would find themselves caught up in such fights.
claims.subject: Chinese tech firms in US-China fights

claims.quote: Mostly, however, we got things wrong.
claims.subject: Overall 2020 record

claims.quote: As expected, there were fights between and within countries about access to vaccines.
claims.subject: Vaccine access disputes

claims.quote: But we failed to foresee just how widespread vaccine refusal would become
claims.subject: Vaccine refusal

claims.quote: Nor did we anticipate the significance of coronavirus “variants”—a word that did not appear in The World in 2021.
claims.subject: Covid variants

claims.quote: In politics, we were right that Donald Trump kept the Republicans in his thrall, and continued to undermine faith in America’s electoral processes.
claims.subject: Trump and the Republican Party

claims.quote: We thought Japan might get a new prime minister, but did not tip Kishida Fumio as a contender.
claims.subject: Japanese prime minister change

claims.quote: We were wrong to suggest demand for oil would stay depressed.
claims.subject: Oil demand

claims.quote: Though we thought the Taliban had “a good chance of returning to power” in Afghanistan, we expected it to be the result of a political deal, not a military clean-sweep.
claims.subject: Taliban return to power

claims.quote: And we were shocked by Xi Jinping’s brutal clampdown on tech companies.
claims.subject: China tech crackdown

claims.quote: We foresaw a growing conflict between autocracy and democracy, but did not expect that conflict to manifest as a shooting war in Europe
claims.subject: Russian invasion of Ukraine

claims.quote: That put paid to the widely held view that the surge in inflation in late 2021 would prove to be transitory—a view we could, in retrospect, have been more sceptical about.
claims.subject: Inflation 2022

claims.quote: As expected, China’s zero-covid policy hampered growth, but Xi Jinping refused to change course.
claims.subject: China zero-covid policy

claims.quote: We correctly predicted Emmanuel Macron’s win in France and Jair Bolsonaro’s loss in Brazil, that “Bongbong” Marcos would prevail in the Philippines, and that the MPLA would hold on in Angola.
claims.subject: Elections in France, Brazil, Philippines and Angola

claims.quote: We also featured Giorgia Meloni as a person to watch, noting that she had “a fighting chance of becoming Italy’s first female prime minister”, as indeed she did after elections in September.
claims.subject: Giorgia Meloni

claims.quote: Our observation that Britain was particularly vulnerable to stagflation was spot on.
claims.subject: UK stagflation

claims.quote: So too was our suggestion that Boris Johnson had more to fear from his own backbench MPs than from the opposition Labour Party; they duly ejected him in July.
claims.subject: Boris Johnson removal

claims.quote: we were right to suggest that Queen Elizabeth II’s platinum jubilee celebrations in June would be the last great spectacle of her reign.
claims.subject: Queen Elizabeth II platinum jubilee

claims.quote: Farther away in space, nasa smashed its dart probe into a small asteroid as expected
claims.subject: NASA DART asteroid impact

claims.quote: The main thing we got wrong in The World Ahead 2023 was being too gloomy about Western economies, predicting a brief recession in America, a deep one in the EU and a long one in Britain during 2023.
claims.subject: Recessions in America, EU and Britain

claims.quote: China’s abrupt dropping of its zero-covid rules in December 2022 also caught us out.
claims.subject: China zero-covid policy

claims.quote: Nor did we predict October’s surprise attack on Israel by Hamas.
claims.subject: Hamas attack on Israel

claims.quote: The war in Ukraine did indeed become a grinding stalemate
claims.subject: War in Ukraine outcome

claims.quote: American politics settled into a Biden-Trump rematch, the BRICS signed up new members, arguments over “ESG” investments intensified and YIMBYs gained ground, all as we expected.
claims.subject: Biden-Trump rematch, BRICS expansion, ESG, YIMBYs

claims.quote: we said Recep Tayyip Erdogan would probably win in Turkey, and Peter Obi would probably lose in Nigeria, much as we might wish otherwise. Sadly we were right on both counts.
claims.subject: Turkish and Nigerian presidential elections

claims.quote: We noted that tensions between Sudan’s president and vice-president “could spell trouble”—and in fact a civil war broke out in April.
claims.subject: Sudan internal conflict

claims.quote: In technology, as anticipated, Apple revealed its mixed-reality headset, the Vision Pro
claims.subject: Apple mixed-reality headset launch

claims.quote: We did not, however, foresee the “iPhone moment” for artificial intelligence (AI), namely the launch of ChatGPT in late November 2022
claims.subject: ChatGPT launch

reviews.readable: first paragraph and standfirst only; rest paywalled

claims.quote: We anticipated none of these extraordinary events.
claims.subject: Biden withdrawal, Trump assassination attempts, Ukraine incursion into Russia, death of Iran's president

claims.quote: And we expected America’s election to be a coin-toss—and failed to foresee the scale of Donald Trump’s decisive victory.
claims.subject: US presidential election 2024
claims.note: The 2024 editor's letter gave Trump "a one-in-three chance".

claims.quote: But several other predictions proved accurate
claims.subject: Other 2024 predictions
claims.note: From the standfirst; the list is paywalled.
